L290@P3: One of the main difficulties in designing the
L291@P3: AANN relies in the selection of the correct number
L292@P3: of nodes that minimizes the loss of information produced in the three hidden layers, and in particular in
L293@P3: the bottleneck layer. Being the AANN designed in
L294@P3: order to minimize the reconstruction error, the best
L295@P3: NN topology can be retrieved by using a simple grid
L296@P3: search algorithm that varies recursively the number
L297@P3: of nodes of the hidden layers and evaluated the
L298@P3: respective error. Then the topology presenting the
L299@P3: lowest error is selected. However, without a starting
L300@P3: point, this approach can be extremely time consuming and a different solution should be found.
L301@P3: Analyzing the structure of the AANN, it can be
L302@P3: found that the number of adjustable parameters in
L303@P3: this kind of networks is:
L304@P3: ð Þ M1 þ M2 ð Þþ d þ k þ 1 d þ k (12)
L305@P3: where M1 and M2 are the numbers of nodes in the
L306@P3: mapping and demapping layers, respectively. The
L307@P3: term d represents the number of nodes of the input/
L308@P3: output layers while the term k refers to the number of
L309@P3: nodes in the bottleneck layer. Equation (12) implies
L310@P3: the following inequality:
L311@P3: M1 þ M2  d n  k
L312@P3: d þ k þ 1 (13)
L313@P3: where n is the number of training samples.
L314@P3: Equation (13) greatly reduces the number of different
L315@P3: AANN configurations to be tested. Aim of a dimensionality reduction method is to reduce the original
L316@P3: spectral dimension into a lower dimensional space.
L317@P3: This can be translated into the AANN structure as:
L318@P3: k  d; n (14)
L319@P3: Once selected the number of nodes in bottleneck
L320@P3: layer, that corresponds to the number of nonlinear
L321@P3: principal components (NLPCs), then Equation (13)
L322@P3: becomes:
L323@P3: M1 þ M2  n (15)
L324@P3: Assuming a balanced structure of the AANN, M1
L325@P3: and M2 should have the same dimensions
L326@P3: (M1 = M2 = M), and Equation (15) can be simplified
L327@P3: as:
L328@P3: 2M  n (16)
L329@P3: Equation (16) is effective only if the number of mapping/demapping nodes M is greater than the number
L330@P3: of nodes in the bottleneck layer k, on the contrary
L331@P3: there will not be enough data to effectively extract k
L332@P3: nonlinear components (Kramer, 1991).
L333@P3: NLPCA applied to hyperspectral images
L334@P3: The NLPCA can be used to project HS images into a
L335@P3: lower dimensional feature space. The training of the
L336@P3: AANN can be performed by using the pixels of the
L337@P3: image, where each band corresponds to one input of
L338@P3: the network. It has to be noted that, as the output has
L339@P3: to simply replicate the input, no independent target
L340@P3: data are provided, and there is no need to have an a
L341@P3: priori knowledge for the implementation of the learning phase. This implies that the AANN training can
L342@P3: be performed in a fully automatic way and that all
L343@P3: pixels in the image can be considered for this task,
L344@P3: which has actually been the technique adopted in this
L345@P3: paper.
L346@P3: Once trained the AANN to perform the identity
L347@P3: mapping, the NLPCs can be obtained directly from
L348@P3: the bottleneck layer. In the same way, the obtained
L349@P3: NLPCs can be subsequently used as input to the
L350@P3: decoding layer in order to obtain the reconstructed
L351@P3: original data. This means that if the training phase of
L352@P3: the AANN finds an acceptable solution, the obtained
L353@P3-4: 378 G. LICCIARDI AND J. CHANUSSOTNLPCs present the same information of the input
L354@P4: data but in a lower dimension. Thus the NLPCA
L355@P4: permits to compress the spectra of the HS images in
L356@P4: few components. Moreover, since the goal of the
L357@P4: supervised training of the AANN is identity map, it
L358@P4: is possible to suppose that the training error E is
L359@P4: associated to the noise. This suggests that the use of
L360@P4: the NLPCA permits to suppress or completely
L361@P4: remove noise and artifacts present in the image.
L362@P4: Noise suppression and spectral dimensionality
L363@P4: reduction can be obtained also with linear PCA.
L364@P4: However, compared to linear decorrelation techniques, NLPCA has many advantages. First of all, with
L365@P4: the PCA or similar approaches the information content is firstly reprojected onto an orthogonal space
L366@P4: and then the obtained components are ordered in
L367@P4: terms of variance. Then the image dimensionality
L368@P4: reduction through PCA can be obtained by discarding the less relevant components in terms of variance.
L369@P4: Since this kind of approaches detect only linear correlations among spectral bands, a relevant part of the
L370@P4: original information can be retained by the last components and consequently lost during the compression phase (Licciardi et al. 2011). From this point of
L371@P4: view, the NLPCA approach has the advantage to
L372@P4: directly compress the original information into an
L373@P4: already defined number of components, allowing an
L374@P4: almost perfect reconstruction of the original data
L375@P4: (Licciardi, Khan, et al., 2012). This characteristic
L376@P4: also has great impact on the distribution of information among components. In fact, differently from
L377@P4: other approaches, in NLPCA the nonlinear components are not ranked in term of variance. This means
L378@P4: that the compressed information tends to be distributed among the components (Licciardi, Del Frate, &
L379@P4: Duca, 2009).
L380@P4: As stated before, the PCA can be obtained using
L381@P4: an AANN without the coding and decoding layers. In
L382@P4: this way it is possible to avoid discarding less relevant
L383@P4: information and project all the information in few
L384@P4: components. However, the main difference between
L385@P4: PCA and NLPCA obtained using AANN is that the
L386@P4: latter is able to map both linear and nonlinear relations between variables, while PCA is only able to
L387@P4: deal with linear ones. This means that, if nonlinear
L388@P4: correlations exist between variables, NLPCA has the
L389@P4: relevant advantage to describe the data with greater
L390@P4: accuracy in fewer components than PCA.
L391@P4: Many methods have been proposed to extract component in a nonlinear manner, for example, locally linear
L392@P4: embedding (LLE) and Isomap (Saul et al. 2004;
L393@P4: Tenenbaum, Silva, & Langford, 2000) visualize highdimensional data by projecting (embedding) them into
L394@P4: a two or three-dimensional space. Principal curves and
L395@P4: self-organizing maps (SOM) (Kohonen, 2001) describe
L396@P4: data by nonlinear curves and nonlinear planes up to two
L397@P4: dimensions. The main limitation of these methods is
L398@P4: related to obtaining low number of features, that may
L399@P4: be not sufficient to describe the inherent information of
L400@P4: the data. An alternative solution to NLPCA can be
L401@P4: offered by the Kernel Principal Components Analysis
L402@P4: (KPCA) (Scholkopf, Smola, & Muller, 1998). In KPCA
L403@P4: the original data are firstly mapped into a higher dimensional feature space F, and then PCA is performed in F to
L404@P4: extract nonlinear PCs of the input data. Due to the high
L405@P4: computational complexity, the mapping into a higher
L406@P4: feature space can be exploited by applying the “kernel
L407@P4: trick” method. The “kernel trick” in machine learning is a
L408@P4: way to easily adapt linear algorithms to nonlinear situations. In the case of KPCA, the kernel trick permits to
L409@P4: project the input data into a higher dimensional implicit
L410@P4: feature space F without having to compute the mapping
L411@P4: explicitly. Similarly to PCA, the dimensionality reduction
L412@P4: is performed by discarding the less relevant components.
L413@P4: Both KPCA and NLPCA methods could be considered
L414@P4: as a nonlinear generalization of the standard PCA and
L415@P4: tend to produce similar results in terms of feature space.
L416@P4: However, being the feature space F implicit and
L417@P4: unknown, is not always possible to find the exact demapping function from F to the original data space (Mika
L418@P4: et al., 1999). The reconstructed data can be obtained by
L419@P4: minimizing the reconstruction error in F with gradient
L420@P4: descent method. Thus, the results obtained with this
L421@P4: approach are quite far from the optimal solution, presenting high amount of spectral distortion and will not
L422@P4: be considered in this paper.
L423@P4: In the literature, NPCA has been proposed as an
L424@P4: effective instrument for dimensionality reduction
L425@P4: and decorrelation of different types of RS data. In
L426@P4: Licciardi & Del Frate (2011) and Licciardi,
L427@P4: Marpu, et al. (2012) NLPCA has been used to reduce
L428@P4: the dimensionality of different HS images, while in
L429@P4: Licciardi & Del Frate (2011), it has been demonstrated the effectiveness of NLPCA on other feature
L430@P4: extraction approaches. Finally, in Licciardi et al.
L431@P4: (2015), the NLPCA has been used to effectively
L432@P4: remove noise from HS data.
L433@P4: Experiments
L434@P4: In this work, we will use the NLPCA approach
L435@P4: described above to process different HS images
L436@P4: related to the main fields of application of spectroscopy. The selected images comprise Earth observation images, biological analysis images as well as
L437@P4: X-ray-microscope images. These datasets present
L438@P4: different characteristics in terms of spectral
L439@P4: range, spatial/spectral resolution, acquisition
L440@P4: mode, and type of noise. In particular we selected:
L441@P4: ● a satellite-borne image, featuring different kind
L442@P4: of noises, mainly produced by the sensor and
L443@P4: the atmosphere;
L444@P4-5: EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF REMOTE SENSING 379● an airborne image, where the effect of the atmosphere can be considered not present, thus presenting only noise from the sensor;
L445@P5: ● a laboratory image that did not present relevant
L446@P5: amount of any kind of noise;
L447@P5: ● an image acquired with a scanning electron
L448@P5: microscope (SEM), featuring no correlation
L449@P5: between bands.
L450@P5: Statistical information of the abovementioned data
L451@P5: are reported in Table 1.
L452@P5: It is important to highlight that, if properly
L453@P5: trained, the same AANN can be used for any images
L454@P5: acquired from the same sensor. This means that is
L455@P5: not necessary to train a new AANN for each image to
L456@P5: be compressed.
L457@P5: For each experiment, in order to satisfy Equation
L458@P5: (16), we trained an AANN using about 60% of the
L459@P5: pixels available (randomly selected) for each image.
L460@P5: Once trained we used the coding network to extract
L461@P5: the NLPCs from the bottleneck layer and we evaluated the compression ratio obtained. The performance of the dimensionality reduction method is
L462@P5: determined in terms of rate and distortion. Rate
L463@P5: essentially measures the percentage or the amount
L464@P5: of compression that can be achieved. In this case
L465@P5: the compression ratio is directly related to the number of nonlinear principal components and is
L466@P5: expressed in terms of bits per pixel per band.
L467@P5: The nonlinear components are then used as input
L468@P5: to the decoding network reconstructing the original
L469@P5: data. The quality of the reconstructed image is evaluated in terms of distortion that can be defined as the
L470@P5: fidelity of the reconstructed data to the original data.
L471@P5: In this study we evaluated the distortion in terms of
L472@P5: SNR, as defined in (Fowler, 2007):
L473@P5: SNR ¼ 10 log10
L474@P5: σ2

L476@P5: where σ2 is the variance of the original image while
L477@P5: MSE is the means square error (MSE) between the
L478@P5: original and the reconstructed image. However, in the
L479@P5: case of real images, noise-free references may not be
L480@P5: available. Thus, the SNR can be derived as the ratio
L481@P5: between the mean value of the pixels in the image,
L482@P5: and the standard deviation of the pixels of a uniform
L483@P5: area in the image:

L488@P5: Ideally, a perfect reconstruction will not remove
L489@P5: noise from the image, thus would not change the
L490@P5: SNR. However, since the NLPCA tends to remove
L491@P5: noise and artifacts from the image, it is expected to
L492@P5: have an improvement of the SNR of the reconstructed image. A further analysis has been exploited
L493@P5: by measuring the spectral distortion introduced by
L494@P5: the compression. This has been obtained by means of
L495@P5: the Spectral Angle Mapper (SAM) algorithm, that
L496@P5: measures the spectral distance between the reconstructed image and the original one:

L505@P5: ROSIS
L506@P5: A first experiment has been performed using an airborne data set acquired by the ROSIS sensor over the
L507@P5: University of Pavia, Italy (Figure 2). Covers the 0.43 μ
L508@P5: to 0.86 μ spectrum with 103 bands having a radiometric resolution of 14 bit. The image represents a
L509@P5: measure of the radiance and being acquired from an
L510@P5: aircraft, the atmospheric contributions noise can be
L511@P5: considered not relevant. The image is mainly affected
L512@P5: by additive noise in the first bands of the detected
L513@P5: spectrum, mainly due to the sensitivity of the detectors. Moreover, the image is also affected by the socalled smile effect, that is a common artifact to
L514@P5: pushbroom-type sensors to which ROSIS belongs.
L515@P5: This effect is caused by optical distortions onto the

L525@P5-6: 380 G. LICCIARDI AND J. CHANUSSOTspatial/spectral detector array which make the instrument spectral response nonuniform for the crosstrack dimension. The consequence of this effect is
L526@P6: that the central wavelength of a band varies with
L527@P6: spatial position across the width of the image in a
L528@P6: smoothly curving pattern. The smile effect producing
L529@P6: an attenuation of the detected signal can be considered as nonlinear noise (Mouroulis, Green, & Chrien,
L530@P6: 2000). The effect of the smile is usually strong on the
L531@P6: bands around atmospheric absorption (760 nm),
L532@P6: however it can’t be detected simply by inspecting
L533@P6: the spectral bands. The most popular technique to
L534@P6: detect if an image is affected by the smile is to analyse
L535@P6: the first components of the Minimum Noise Fraction
L536@P6: (MNF) (Dadon, Ben-Dor, & Karnieli, 2010).
L537@P6: The image has 340 × 610 pixels, and 120,000
L538@P6: samples have been used to train the AANN. In this
L539@P6: experiment, we evaluated several configurations of
L540@P6: the bottleneck layer in order to detect the best
L541@P6: trade-off between SNR and compression. However,
L542@P6: in order to concentrate our attention on the compression side, we analyzed only the performances
L543@P6: obtained varying the number of nodes in the
L544@P6: bottleneck. For this reason we choose in accordance
L545@P6: with Equation (16) the same number of nodes
L546@P6: (M = 30) in the coding and decoding layers, for all
L547@P6: the different configurations.
L548@P6: The training phase of the different AANNs has
L549@P6: been performed using 60% of the 120,000 pixels in
L550@P6: the image. For each AANN, the training has been
L551@P6: considered complete when the sum of square error
L552@P6: expressed in Equation (2) is minimized. The training
L553@P6: performance has been evaluated in terms of MSE
L554@P6: computed on the complete dataset.
L555@P6: Figures 3 and 4 report the SAM and SNR values
L556@P6: for the PCA and NLPCA approaches as the number
L557@P6: of component varies. Analyzing the distortion performances of PCA and NLPCA reported in Table 2 it
L558@P6: can be noted that NLPCA reaches the best trade-off
L559@P6: between distortion and compression with 4 components, while PCA saturates the SNR and SAM with
L560@P6: just three components, but with a quality of the
L561@P6: reconstructed image comparable to the one obtained
L562@P6: using NLPCA. This can be explained by the non
L563@P6: completely linear behavior of the investigated image.

L589@P7: the smile effect. Analyzing the MNF components

L613@P8: Hyperion
L614@P8: In a second experiment, we applied the proposed
L615@P8: method to a Hyperion image acquired in 2008 over
L616@P8: the Campi Flegrei area, North-West of Naples, Italy.
L617@P8: Hyperion features 242 bands from 0.4 μm to 2.5 μm
L618@P8: with a radiometric resolution of 12 bit. Differently
L619@P8: from the previous experiment, in this case the image
L620@P8: has been acquired from a satellite. This means that
L621@P8: the atmospheric contribution has a relevant role in
L622@P8: terms of noise of the image. For this reason atmospheric correction has been applied and the data
L623@P8: converted into reflectance at ground level. Similar to
L624@P8: the ROSIS instrument, Hyperion is a pushbroom type
L625@P8: sensor, meaning that it could be affected by the smile
L626@P8: effect. Moreover, the Hyperion instrument is characterized by poorly calibrated detectors, that is the
L627@P8: result of small variations in the gain of each column
L628@P8: of detectors. These detectors cause high frequency
L629@P8: errors in the VNIR or SWIR regions, which can be
L630@P8: identified as vertical strips in the image bands. These
L631@P8: stripping errors can affect the mean and standard
L632@P8: deviation of the data values for particular Hyperion
L633@P8: band. Before compressing the Hyperion image a preprocessing step to remove the most noisy bands not
L634@P8: containing relevant information has been performed
L635@P8: on the original dataset, resulting in 155 spectrally
L636@P8: unique and good quality bands (Datt, Vicar, Niel,
L637@P8: Jupp, & Pearlman, 2003).
L638@P8: The considered image consists of 100 × 100 pixels,
L639@P8: and also this time we trained the AANNs using 60%
L640@P8: of all the pixels from the image. Also in this experiment we evaluated the performances of the NLPCA
L641@P8: dimensionality reduction method by varying only the
L642@P8: number of nodes in the bottleneck. In particular, the
L643@P8: number of nodes in the coding/decoding layers has
L644@P8: been chosen to be 50 for all the configurations.
L645@P8: Similarly to the previous experiment, the rate-distortion of the NLPCA dimensionality reduction method
L646@P8: has been evaluated in terms of SNR and spectral
L647@P8: distortion and compared with the performance of the
L648@P8: standard PCA. Figures 7 and 8 report the SNR and
L649@P8: SAM values as the number of components varies for
L650@P8: PCA and NLPCA, respectively. Analyzing these curves
L651@P8: it can be noted that the best tradeoff between spectral
L652@P8: compression and quality of the reconstructed image is
L653@P8: obtained with nine components. Analyzing the values
L654@P8: reported in Table 3 it is also evident that with the
L655@P8: PCA approach it is possible to obtain a similar quality
L656@P8: with 30 components.
L657@P8: In Figure 9 the reconstructed images, obtained
L658@P8: using only nine components for PCA and NLPCA,
L659@P8: are depicted. As expected, both PCA and NLPCA
L660@P8: performed as noise filters for the input image.
L661@P8: However, a further analysis can be carried out by
L662@P8: inspecting the bands where both linear and nonlinear
L663@P8: noise is present. More in particular, while in band 1
L664@P8: only additive noise is present, band 88 is affected also
L665@P8: by the striping. Thus, due to its linear nature, PCA is
L666@P8: not able to filter all the noises present in band 88, as it
L667@P8: is possible with NLPCA.

L670@P8-9: EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF REMOTE SENSING 383Hyspex
L671@P9: A third experiment has been conducted using a field
L672@P9: HS image. In particular we analyzed the performance
L673@P9: of the NLPCA dimensionality reduction on a Hyspex
L674@P9: image acquired on the field for the biochemical
L675@P9: analysis of the vegetation. The considered Hyspex is
L676@P9: a pushbroom sensor with a spectral coverage within
L677@P9: 0.4–1.0 μm, for a total of 160 bands having radiometric resolution of 12 bit. Before being processed
L678@P9: the image has been converted to reflectance. In this
L679@P9: case, the sensor has been mounted on a tripod very
L680@P9: close to the target vegetation (1m). The static nature
L681@P9: of the support reduced to the minimum the amount
